top.line: A monthly-rent plan for AI-built websites gets the economics wrong; sell a finished job and let the client own the stack.
top.para: An infographic proposed £39 to £119 monthly plans with page and edit caps and the seller's Claude subscription as the main cost. Rent pays most when clients use least, and a few clients never stop asking. Instead, the client owns an AI account, GitHub Pages and a domain, and pays once for setup, build, design choice, QA and handover.

in-short.line: Rent pays you for non-use; page caps are arbitrary; the client should own the stack and buy a finished job.
in-short.para: Monthly plans reward low use and let a few clients drain you. Static pages cost almost nothing, so caps make no sense. The client should own Claude or ChatGPT, GitHub Pages and a domain, pay once for setup, build, designs, QA and handover, and buy blocks of hours only if wanted.

infographic.line: An infographic from someone being helped; it carries no author data, and it still proposed rent.
infographic.para: The sender's agent read the newsroom first yet still produced a rent business, so this article states the position in one place. The image's metadata holds only resolution and orientation, and nothing in it identifies the author. The instinct is good; the model underneath is the problem.

plans.line: Page caps of five or ten are a pricing device, and a monthly edit allowance keeps the client dependent.
plans.para: Pages cost almost nothing with an agent and a static host; this newsroom runs about 1,500 on GitHub Pages, limited to a 1 GB site and 100 GB of monthly bandwidth. The real limit is the client's tokens. Thirty minutes of edits a month stops clients changing their own sites. Client ownership of domain and content is right.

cost.line: The seller's Claude subscription puts cost and bottleneck in the wrong place; GitHub Pages bars online shops.
cost.para: Clients can hold their own AI account, which they may already pay for, and reselling AI access may carry legal risk. Static hosting is right and free on GitHub Pages, but GitHub's terms bar using Pages to run an online business that facilitates transactions or SaaS, so shops need another static host.

time.line: Ten to fifteen hours a build, mostly not code: price the client's time, as a finished job.
time.para: Calls, content, revisions and launch take most of the time, and pricing on the client's time rather than the agent's speed is right. That argues for pricing the work as a finite job, delivered and finished.

numbers.line: The arithmetic holds only at the low cost end, and the incentive punishes use.
numbers.para: £1,127 for one client in year one is right. Two clients cover fixed costs only at £95, not £190, and ten clients leave about £570 only at the lowest costs, nearer £450 at the top. On monthly plans margins fall as use rises, and around 10 to 15 per cent of clients treat the fee as permission to ask endlessly.

risks.line: Keeping sites static is right; usage caps are only a risk because the seller holds one AI account.
risks.para: Reading what the agent writes and keeping sites static is sound. When each client has their own AI account, the cap is theirs and no same-hour promise is needed.

model.line: Charge once for setup, build, design choice, QA and handover; then blocks of hours; prices set by the market.
model.para: Wire the client's AI account, GitHub and domain together; build from their documents with designs to choose from; teach them to edit by talking to their AI. Sell a domain for a year as a one-off, help as hour blocks, and lift-and-shift conversions. Finite engagements leave clients in control and telling others: explorer services built on open source.

mockup.line: Kitewing Websites, a made-up studio with three made-up client sites, shows the model working.
mockup.para: The agents built a studio site and three client sites, a potter's catalogue, a community garden and a plumber's guides library, each as a vault app; the tour is a separate article.

limits.line: The infographic's figures are its author's; the percentage is experience; prices are hypotheses.
limits.para: Only the arithmetic was checked, not the costs. Reselling AI access may be allowed under some terms, which were not checked, so it should not be depended on.

sources.line: The infographic, a voice memo, GitHub's Pages limits and terms, and related newsroom articles.
sources.para: The infographic of 26 October 2026, the editor's memo, GitHub Docs on Pages limits and GitHub's terms for Pages, read that day, plus articles on subscriptions, paying after value, finite jobs, explorer coding and the newsroom recipe.
